# SURVEY_ENGINEERING.md
## Faculty of Engineering — Initial Site / Feasibility Survey

**Status:** Independent early feasibility survey (planning phase)
**Site:** Hillside plot, ~80 m across-slope × 100 m up-slope, ~18 m fall low→high edge (~18% average grade)
**Brief:** Lecture halls/classrooms for a mid-sized faculty, staff offices, cafeteria/canteen for students and staff.

> This is a first-pass feasibility survey, not a design. All dimensions, materials and
> strategies below are proposals to be tested by survey, geotechnical investigation and
> cost study. Nothing here is fixed by anyone else; the choices are mine and are stated
> as such.

---

## 1. Reading the Site

The defining fact is the **18 m fall over 100 m up-slope** — an average grade of ~18%,
with local variation likely steeper. This is not a site that can be "flattened"; it is a
site that must be **stepped**. Three consequences drive everything else:

1. **Earthworks are the dominant cost and risk.** Cut-and-fill to create a single level
   platform would require enormous cut at the uphill edge and enormous fill at the
   downhill edge, with a high retaining structure and a large unstable fill mass. I reject
   a single-platform solution.
2. **Water runs downhill and will run toward the building.** Surface-water management is
   not an add-on; it is a primary design driver.
3. **Access gradients are constrained.** A continuous 18% route is at/over the practical
   limit for accessible pedestrian ramps and is steep for vehicles. Circulation must be
   broken into stepped, gentler segments.

### 1.1 Approach to terrain — "terrace and bridge, don't flatten"

My approach is **terrace the building into the slope** and use the natural fall as an
organising device rather than fighting it:

- **Step the building down the slope in 3–4 terraces**, each terrace a level floor plate
  of roughly 4–6 m fall. This keeps cut and fill roughly balanced *locally* at each
  terrace, minimising imported fill and exported spoil.
- **Cut-and-fill balance per terrace** is the target: cut into the uphill side of each
  terrace, use that material to build up the downhill side, so net haulage across the site
  is small. Any surplus spoil is stockpiled for landscaping/berms, not exported if
  avoidable.
- **Retaining walls** at each terrace edge. Working assumption: reinforced-concrete
  cantilever or counterfort walls for the taller steps (up to ~5–6 m), with
  **soil-nailed or anchored** solutions where the wall must also stabilise the slope
  behind it. Wall type is to be confirmed by geotechnical investigation.
- **Drainage-first design:** an interception drain (cut-off drain) *above* the uphill edge
  of the works to divert upslope catchment away from the building; a network of
  surface-water channels and a below-ground drainage blanket behind every retaining wall
  to relieve hydrostatic pressure; and a positive gravity outfall to the low edge of the
  site. No water is allowed to pond against a wall or sit under a floor slab.
- **Slope stability:** the geotechnical brief must establish the existing factor of
  safety, the effect of cutting the toe and loading the terraces, and whether ground
  improvement, anchoring or piling is needed. I assume **no construction starts before a
  slope-stability assessment** is complete.

### 1.2 Access and circulation

- **Vehicles:** a one-way loop or a single access road climbing the slope at a controlled
  gradient, entering at the low edge and serving each terrace level. Service/delivery
  access to the cafeteria is at the lowest terrace to keep heavy vehicles off the steep
  upper ramps.
- **Pedestrians:** the primary vertical movement is by **stepped terraces and stairs**,
  with **lifts** connecting all levels. An accessible route is provided as a series of
  ramps at compliant gradients (broken into landings) or, where the fall is too great, by
  lift. I do **not** rely on a single long ramp at 18%.
- **Parking** is placed at the low (downhill) edge where the ground is closest to level,
  minimising cut/fill and keeping the steep upper terraces for building and quiet uses.

---

## 2. Zoning / Footprint Concept

The building is conceived as a **stepped spine** running up-slope, with the noisiest and
most public functions at the bottom and the quietest at the top.

| Terrace | Level (relative) | Function | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 (low edge) | ±0 m | **Cafeteria/canteen**, service yard, deliveries, parking | Heaviest servicing, most public, easiest vehicle access, best daylight and views; keeps food deliveries off steep ramps. |
| T2 | ~ -4 to -5 m | **Lecture halls / large classrooms**, main student concourse, main entrance from mid-slope | High-traffic teaching near the main pedestrian arrival; large-span halls suit a terrace with a deep cut behind. |
| T3 | ~ -9 to -10 m | **Classrooms, seminar rooms, teaching labs** | Mid-slope, quieter, flexible room sizes. |
| T4 (high edge) | ~ -14 to -18 m | **Staff offices, administration, library/study** | Quietest, best views, least public traffic; offices benefit from the stable cut side. |

**Footprint logic:**
- Building footprint is **narrow in the up-slope direction** (so each terrace is a shallow
  cut/fill band) and **long across-slope** (using the 80 m width). This keeps retaining
  heights moderate and daylight reach into every floor plate.
- A **central circulation spine** (stairs + lifts + concourse) runs across-slope and
  connects the terraces, doubling as the accessible vertical route.
- **Courtyards / light wells** are cut into the terraces between wings to bring daylight
  and air into deep floor plates and to break the building into smaller, slope-friendly
  blocks.
- **Roofs** step with the terraces, giving usable terraces/plant zones and reducing the
  apparent height of the building against the hill.

Rough order-of-magnitude: a mid-sized faculty of this brief plausibly needs on the order
of **8,000–12,000 m² gross floor area**; at 3–4 terraces this is a footprint of roughly
**2,500–3,500 m² per terrace band**, comfortably within the 80 m × 100 m plot once
circulation, courtyards and access are allowed for. (To be refined against the room
schedule.)

---

## 3. Primary Construction Materials — Building Generally

Given the steep site, the retaining structures, and the need for robustness and
maintainability, my primary proposal is a **reinforced-concrete frame with a masonry/
concrete envelope**, with steel used selectively for long-span roofs.

**Structure — reinforced concrete (RC) frame, in-situ:**
- Best fit for a terraced building on a slope: RC frames integrate naturally with the
  retaining walls and foundations, handle the irregular grid the terraces impose, and give
  the mass and stiffness needed where floors step and where walls retain soil.
- Good fire performance and durability with minimal additional protection — important for
  a public building.
- Foundations: likely **pad/raft on the cut side and piled or deep foundations on the fill
  side**, confirmed by geotechnical investigation.

**Where steel is preferred:** long-span **lecture hall roofs** and any large column-free
spans, where a steel truss/portal frame is lighter and faster than RC. Steel is protected
with intumescent coating or board to achieve the required fire rating.

**Envelope:**
- **External walls:** insulated cavity masonry or concrete with a rainscreen/cladding
  finish; robust, low-maintenance, and tolerant of a damp hillside environment.
- **Roofs:** warm flat roofs with a durable membrane (e.g. single-ply) and generous
  drainage falls; stepped roofs drained to the terrace below.
- **Glazing:** thermally broken aluminium or timber-aluminium frames, double/triple
  glazed; shading to control solar gain on the exposed slope.

**Why not a lightweight/timber-primary building here?** Timber is attractive for carbon
and speed, and I would use it for internal partitions, some roofs and fit-out — but a
slope site with heavy retaining and foundation demands, plus the fire and robustness
requirements of a public teaching building, make an RC primary frame the lower-risk
choice for the *first* feasibility pass. This is a judgement, and a hybrid RC/timber
scheme is worth testing at the next stage.

---

## 4. Cafeteria / Canteen — Specific Materials

The cafeteria sits at the lowest terrace (T1) and has the most demanding combination of
requirements: **structural span, fire rating, hygiene, moisture resistance, and
maintenance**. My proposal:

**Structure / span:**
- The dining area wants **long, column-free spans** for flexibility. I propose a
  **steel roof structure** (portal or truss) over the dining hall to achieve spans of
  ~12–18 m without deep RC beams, supported on RC columns/walls. Kitchen and servery use
  the standard RC frame with a tighter grid.
- Floor: **reinforced-concrete slab on grade / suspended slab** with a fall to drains.

**Fire rating:**
- The cafeteria is a high-occupancy, high-fire-load space (cooking + large numbers of
  people). Structure and separating walls to be rated to the code requirement for the
  occupancy (working assumption **60–90 minutes** for structure and compartmentation,
  confirmed against the applicable code). Steel roof members protected by intumescent
  coating or fire-rated board; RC elements inherently achieve the rating.
- **Kitchen is a separate fire compartment** with rated walls/doors and its own
  suppression (assumed sprinkler + kitchen hood suppression).

**Hygiene (the decisive driver):**
- **Floors:** seamless, non-slip, coved **epoxy or resin screed** (or welded-sheet vinyl
  in dining areas) — impervious, easily cleaned, with coved skirting to walls so there are
  no dirt traps.
- **Walls (kitchen/servery):** smooth, washable, impervious — **ceramic/porcelain tiling**
  or hygienic wall cladding to full height behind cooking and prep areas.
- **Ceilings (kitchen):** wipeable, moisture-resistant panels with sealed joints; services
  kept out of food areas or fully enclosed.
- **Dining area:** more forgiving finishes (durable vinyl or timber-look flooring, painted
  or clad walls) but still hard-wearing and cleanable.

**Moisture resistance:**
- Kitchens are wet, steamy environments. I specify **moisture-resistant boards and
  impervious finishes**, sealed penetrations, and **mechanical extract with make-up air**
  to control humidity and grease-laden vapour. Floor build-ups include a **tanked/
  waterproofed layer** and trapped drainage.
- Being at the low terrace, the cafeteria is the most exposed to groundwater and surface
  run-off: **tanking to the below-ground walls and slab**, a perimeter drainage channel,
  and a floor level set above the external ground/outfall.

**Maintenance:**
- All finishes chosen for **easy repair and cleaning**: replaceable tile/cladding panels,
  resin floors that can be re-coated, accessible service voids, and robust, cleanable
  surfaces. Stainless steel is used for kitchen equipment and worktops (hygienic,
  corrosion-resistant, long-lived).

**Summary of cafeteria materials:**
| Element | Proposal |
|---|---|
| Dining-hall structure | Steel portal/truss roof on RC columns, 12–18 m clear span |
| Kitchen structure | RC frame, tighter grid |
| Fire | 60–90 min rated structure/compartmentation; separate rated kitchen compartment; sprinklers + hood suppression |
| Floors | Coved, seamless resin/epoxy (kitchen); durable vinyl (dining) |
| Walls | Full-height tiling / hygienic cladding (kitchen); hard-wearing cleanable finish (dining) |
| Ceilings | Moisture-resistant, wipeable, sealed (kitchen) |
| Moisture | Tanking, trapped drainage, mechanical extract, floor above outfall |
| Equipment | Stainless steel |

---

## 5. Key Risks and Open Questions

1. **Slope stability** — the single biggest risk. Requires a geotechnical investigation
   (boreholes, slope-stability analysis) before any commitment. Cutting the toe and
   loading terraces could reduce the factor of safety; anchoring/piling may be required.
2. **Retaining wall heights and types** — driven by the terrace strategy; to be confirmed
   with geotechnics and structural design.
3. **Drainage capacity and outfall** — where does the site discharge to, and can it take
   the upslope catchment plus the site's own run-off? Attenuation may be needed.
4. **Access gradients** — confirm the accessible route strategy (ramps + lifts) against
   the applicable accessibility standard.
5. **Cut/fill balance and spoil** — confirm volumes; minimise export.
6. **Foundations on fill** — the downhill (fill) side will need careful foundation design;
   piling may be needed.
7. **Cost** — earthworks, retaining and foundations will be a large share of the budget;
   the terrace strategy is chosen partly to control this, but it must be costed.
8. **Code confirmation** — fire ratings, occupancy and accessibility figures are working
   assumptions pending the applicable local code.

---

## 6. Conclusion

The site is buildable but **demanding**. My approach is to **work with the slope, not
against it**: step the building down in terraces with balanced local cut-and-fill,
stabilise and drain the slope as a first-order concern, and organise the faculty so that
servicing and public functions sit at the accessible low edge and quiet functions at the
stable high edge. The primary structure is a **reinforced-concrete frame** (with steel for
long spans), and the **cafeteria** is a steel-roofed, RC-framed, fully tanked and
hygienically finished space with a rated, separately-compartmented kitchen. All of this is
a first feasibility position to be tested by survey, geotechnical investigation and cost
study.

**Status: complete.**
